title: Ezra 4:1–6
context: News of the building reaches those the narrator calls the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin. They offer to build alongside the returned exiles, saying they have sought the same God and sacrificed to him since the days of Esar Haddon king of Assyria, who brought them there (4:1–2). Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the heads of households refuse, appealing to the command of Cyrus (4:3; compare 1:2–3). The people of the land then discourage and trouble the builders and hire counselors against them through the reign of Cyrus until the reign of Darius (4:4–5), and in the beginning of the reign of Ahasuerus they write an accusation (4:6). Background and related notices, named without harmonization: 2 Kings 17:24–41 tells how the king of Assyria settled peoples in the cities of Samaria who feared the LORD and also served their own gods, though that chapter does not name Esar Haddon. The kings named in chapter 4 appear in this order: Cyrus and Darius (4:5), Ahasuerus (4:6), Artaxerxes (4:7–23), and then Darius again (4:24). Many readers take 4:6–23 as a thematic digression that gathers later episodes of opposition before 4:24 resumes the Darius-era story; others arrange the material differently. This commentary describes the sequence as the text gives it and does not fix these kings to a reconstructed timeline or connect this Ahasuerus with another book. Both traditions read the opposition soberly and see God’s providence at work through it.

verses.text: Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the children of the captivity were building a temple to the LORD, the God of Israel,
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator calls these neighbors the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin, a label that anticipates their later conduct. Arminian readers note that opposition arises when the people begin to obey, and that faithfulness in God’s work often meets resistance that must be met with patience rather than with resentment or caricature of opponents.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see opposition to the rebuilding as something the LORD permits and governs, so that even adversaries serve his larger purposes in the story of the temple. Shared ground: both traditions affirm God’s providence through opposition and both read the adversaries as accountable people, not as cartoon villains, whose actions the narrative will report at length.

verses.text: they came near to Zerubbabel, and to the heads of fathers’ households, and said to them, “Let us build with you, for we seek your God as you do; and we have been sacrificing to him since the days of Esar Haddon king of Assyria, who brought us up here.”
verses.arminianNotes: The neighbors offer to build, claiming to seek the same God and to have sacrificed to him since Esar Haddon brought them there. Arminian readers take the offer seriously as their own account of themselves, while noting that 2 Kings 17:33 and 17:41 describe the settlers of Samaria as fearing the LORD and also serving their own gods, which makes shared building a real question.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that true worship is defined by what God has revealed and not only by sincere profession, so a claim to seek the same God must be weighed against the worship actually practiced. Shared ground: both traditions note that the text does not state the motives of these neighbors beyond the narrator’s label, and both caution against reading more into their hearts than the passage gives.

verses.text: But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of fathers’ households of Israel said to them, “You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God; but we ourselves together will build to the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us.”
verses.arminianNotes: Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the heads of households decline, appealing to the decree of Cyrus, which addressed the LORD’s own people (Ezra 1:3). Arminian readers see a concern to protect the community’s covenant identity and the specific mandate given to them, while remembering that the prophets also look for foreigners who truly join themselves to the LORD (Isaiah 56:6–7).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the refusal as guarding the purity of worship against a mixed religion, in a setting where Israel’s exile had followed long unfaithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions see the narrative presenting the refusal as faithfulness to God and to Cyrus’s command, and both hold that Scripture elsewhere welcomes all peoples who seek the LORD (compare Zechariah 8:20–23).

verses.text: Then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building.
verses.arminianNotes: The people of the land weaken the hands of the people of Judah and trouble them in building. Arminian readers note that discouragement is real and can slow obedient people, so perseverance is a genuine calling and not an automatic outcome, and they observe the reversal at Ezra 6:22, where the LORD strengthens the people’s hands in the work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see weakened hands as a trial God allows, and they also point to Ezra 6:22, where the LORD turns a king’s heart to strengthen their hands, showing that he governs both the delay and the recovery. Shared ground: both traditions read discouragement and renewed strength as part of the same providential story, and both counsel endurance under opposition.

verses.text: They hired counselors against them to frustrate their purpose all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia.
verses.arminianNotes: Hired counselors frustrate the builders’ purpose through the days of Cyrus until the reign of Darius. Arminian readers note that human opposition can really hinder good work for a long time, and that Haggai 1:2–4 also points to the people’s own neglect, so the delay had more than one cause and called for genuine repentance and renewed effort.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the long delay as falling within God’s purposes, who later stirs up the leaders and people through Haggai (Haggai 1:14) to resume the work. Shared ground: both traditions read the delay as involving both outside opposition and the community’s own failings, and both see the LORD as the one who renews the work in his time.

verses.text: In the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: In the beginning of the reign of Ahasuerus the adversaries write an accusation against Judah and Jerusalem, though its contents are not given. Arminian readers note that opposition recurs under successive rulers, so faithfulness must be renewed in each generation and cannot rest on one season of success or one favorable decree.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the repeated accusations that God’s people are kept through many changes of rulers, and that no accusation falls outside his rule. Shared ground: both traditions read this brief notice, which many take as the start of a thematic survey of later opposition, as a reminder of persistent resistance to God’s work, without needing to fix its exact date.
